value: to move Helen into the room where her sister died

reasoning.text: Within a month of her engagement the repairs pierce her wall, and the bride-to-be has to sleep where the last bride-to-be died, next to Dr. Roylott's room.

value: to give a way from the opening down to the bed

reasoning.text: With no wire it does nothing as a bell, but it runs from just above the little opening down to the pillow.

value: to keep the bed always in the same position to the ventilator and the rope
quote: It must always be in the same relative position to the ventilator and to the rope

goal.value: always in the same relative position to the ventilator and to the rope

rule.value: always in the same relative position to the ventilator and to the rope
always in the same relative position to the ventilator and to the rope

why: This is not an aim served by an action. The unused half of the return ticket at ¶14 tells against flight, and Helen says at ¶81 that she will go back by the twelve o'clock train.

The reader reaches it through the money: the income passes to her on marriage (¶17, ¶25), and the will's figures at ¶115 show what a marriage would cost the holder. It is the end of the chain, and at ¶20 no agent is yet known to hold the aim.

The motive is reached by the provision for each daughter (¶25), the timing of Julia's death just before her wedding (¶30), and the sums from the will that Holmes gives at ¶115. It is the end of the chain and is raised with no agent known, so naming one in the entry would run ahead of the story.

The reader reaches it by the parallel at ¶67, by Holmes's remark on the sound end wall at ¶135, and by Helen's belief at ¶136. The aim has no named agent in its own question. Its reasoning instead adds a need that lets the circled answer to who ordered the repairs link to Roylott's aim.

It is reached by what is found and told about the room: the sham rope and the ventilator (¶149-153), then the clamped bed and Holmes's account of its fixed position (¶214-216). No action of a named agent is being explained here.

It is reached by place and not by aim. The narrator says the lantern was lit in the next room (¶236), Holmes has already said that 'he' would see a light through the ventilator (¶229), and that room is Roylott's.

It is reached by a light and a place: the whistle sounds as the match is struck in a shuttered room (¶238), and only someone beyond the ventilator could see that light (¶229). The recall purpose is told only at ¶248, and putting the snake in an entry raised at ¶36 would run ahead of the story.

The dummy rope, its hook above the opening and the fixed bed are told at ¶149-151 and ¶214-216, and Holmes gives the purpose at ¶248. The question has no agent of its own; its reasoning adds a need that lets the circled answer to who put in the fittings link to Roylott's aim.

It is reached by the told oddity that it opens into another room and not to the outside air (¶153), by its tie to the rope and the fixed bed (¶216), and by Holmes's explanation at ¶248. No who-question on making the opening offers an action to link.
It is reached by place and household: the saucer stands on the safe in his own bedroom, the house keeps no cat, and Helen knows nothing of it (¶165-166). What the milk is for is told only at ¶248.

It is reached by matching two told facts: Indian animals are sent to Roylott by a correspondent (¶27), and the snake is named as Indian (¶245). Holmes confirms the supply at ¶248; the supply serves no aim that is on the timeline before then.
